source: Copyhackers, Seven Sweeps tutorial (Sweeps 3 So What + 4 Prove It), Asana home page
before: Asana is the easiest way for teams to track their work, complete tasks, and get results.
after: No rewrite; direction: keep the line (it passes So What via 'get results') but attach a data point for 'results' (e.g., a project-time statistic) and proof of 'easiest'
quote_status: before verbatim; after paraphrase of stated direction
defect_named: Passes So What, fails Prove It: 'easy' and 'get results' are asserted, not proven
principle: Every claim gets a Prove It sweep: a number, a demo or a logo within reach of the claim
reason: Wiebe runs the sweeps line by line and highlights any claim with no proof beside it (paraphrase of tutorial).

source: Copyhackers, Seven Sweeps tutorial (Sweeps 3 + 4), Asana home page
before: Finish short and long-term projects together. See how creating and moving projects forward in Asana will help your team. You'll know who is doing what and when they're doing it.
after: No rewrite; direction: answer 'so what if I know who is doing what?' and replace the static screenshot with a GIF, video or autoplay demo that shows it
quote_status: before verbatim (one duplicated word removed); after paraphrase of stated direction
defect_named: 'So what if I know who is doing what and when they're doing it?' (verbatim); the screenshot is 'a perfectly nice screen shot' but proves nothing
principle: Each feature line must carry its consequence for the reader and a proof object that shows the feature working
reason: Whole section highlighted for failing So What; Prove It fails because a screenshot cannot prove the claim (paraphrase).

source: Copyhackers, Seven Sweeps tutorial (Sweeps 3 + 4), Asana home page
before: Get started today. If you can make a list or send an email you can use Asana. Starting a team is really that simple.
after: No rewrite; direction: say what happens next ('Next you'll invite your team'), prove how easy adding team members is, and consider a click trigger near the button about the next steps
quote_status: before verbatim; after paraphrase with one verbatim fragment
defect_named: So What is 'not wrong, but it's not right either' (verbatim); 'really that simple' is unproven and the list/email line does not connect to it
principle: A claim of ease is proven by showing the next step, not by asserting simplicity
reason: Prove It fails on 'that simple'; the fix is to show the first action after the click (paraphrase).

source: Copyhackers, Seven Sweeps tutorial (Sweep 7 Zero Risk), Asana home page headline
before: Move Work Forward
after: No rewrite; highlighted but left unchanged because the big idea is unknown: 'I don't know what their big idea should be'
defect_named: 'it's not clear, it's not specific' (verbatim); no So What, no Prove It, not emotional, no risk reduction, no voice: 'zero of any Sweeps at all'
principle: A headline that fails every sweep cannot be edited; it is a big-idea problem to be solved upstream
reason: Wiebe refuses to rewrite a headline without first knowing the big idea; the sweeps edit copy, they do not choose the argument (paraphrase).

source: Copyhackers, Seven Sweeps tutorial (Voice and Tone sweep), Asana home page
before: You can set aggressive goals. ... and actually hit them.
after: Your team's responsibilities and next steps are clear so you can set lofty goals ... and actually reach them.
defect_named: Word choice off the intended voice: 'aggressive' and 'hit' do not sound friendly, calm or smart
principle: Edit single words against the voice profile's named attributes, not against taste
reason: 'lofty' may sound friendlier; 'reach them' judged friendly, calm and smart (paraphrase). Also tied the claim to clear responsibilities.

source: Copyhackers, 'How to be specific in your copywriting' (Wistia onboarding email)

reason: Specific headline lets the uninterested skip and the interested keep reading (paraphrase).

tested.result: Whole 8-email Wistia sequence: 3.5x paid conversions vs control (same test as v0 P06-P09); this line not isolated

source: Copyhackers, Heightened Emotion sweep tutorial (Talia Wolf on Gusto)

source: AWAI, Guillermo Rubio on Clayton Makepeace's dimensionalizing method
before: Constructed of carbon steel. (feature) / Never wears out. (why)

principle: Feature, purpose, benefit, then dimensionalize: what it means in the prospect's life, in money, time and feeling
reason: People buy on emotion and justify with logic; the strongest copy reaches the underlying want (paraphrase). The $75 is a sample claim, not a result.

source: VeryGoodCopy, 'Could this be the worst sales email ever written?'

after: No rewrite; fix: explain each term or cut it, and state what the reader gains early

principle: Clear beats clever; the reader's gain before the sender's description
reason: The recipient CEO shared the email on social as an example of what not to do.

principle: 'Ads make promises. Promises bring people hope. Don't fuck with a person's hope.' (verbatim)
reason: Maps to the claims ledger: a statistic with no source is a hard reject.

source: VeryGoodCopy, '26 words you can almost always simplify'

after: LANDFILL

source: VeryGoodCopy, 'Confident copy connects and converts'
before: Hedging qualifiers: generally, probably, often, most; passive voice that avoids 'specifying authority'; vague or ambiguous claims
after: Bold, direct statements that commit, e.g. the mirror sticker 'GET IT BECAUSE YOU WANT IT.'
defect_named: Equivocation: copy that is 'vague or ambiguous or uncertain' (verbatim)
principle: No hedges on supported claims; copy says 'you're making the right decision'

source: Ship 30 for 30, 'Clear vs Clever'
before: We deliver asynchronous reporting data and analytics to integrate your business into the creator economy's growing community.
after: Sales Analytics For Creators.
defect_named: Jargon that sounds smart but does not say what the company does
principle: Describe the solution in five words or fewer; if you cannot, you are not clear on what you sell

source: Ship 30 for 30, 'Clear vs Clever'
before: For People. With People. By People.
after: No rewrite; state what the company does
defect_named: 'Clever' chosen over 'clear': wordplay at the top of the site; confused readers leave
principle: Clarity first; cleverness only when the reader already knows what you sell
reason: Also flagged: 'Unleash your creativity...', 'Real-time changes, real-time trust...', 'Big Problem? You Betcha.'

source: Ship 30 for 30, '7 Copywriting Mistakes Hurting Your Course Sales'
before: Learn how to...
after: Promise what buyers will do, experience and unlock (no verbatim rewrite)
defect_named: Leading with 'learn': buyers want the outcome, not the learning process
principle: Sell the result, not the curriculum
reason: Authors report 'a clear increase in sales every time we fixed one of these problems' on their own page (no figures).

tested.result: self-reported sales increase, no figure

source: Ship 30 for 30, '7 Copywriting Mistakes'
before: Here's what you get!
after: Benefits in headlines, outcomes in descriptions; page ordered as struggle, solution, changed life, sign-up
defect_named: Focusing on features; 'solutions before problems' (customers cannot care about a solution before the problem)
principle: Problem before solution; benefit before feature

tested.result: same self-reported page result

source: Ship 30 for 30, 'How to Write a Twitter Thread Using Hooks' (thought experiment)
before: College completely failed in teaching me how to write. (hook without the contrast line)
after: College completely failed in teaching me how to write. ... But unlike college, these won't cost you $120,000.
defect_named: Without the contrast the hook 'loses its sting'; the free offer no longer contrasts with the $120,000 cost
principle: A contrast line with a number makes the free thing feel valuable
reason: Author calls it 'one of my most successful threads ever' (no metrics).

tested.result: self-described top thread, no metric

source: John Forde, Copywriter's Roundtable, 'How One Big Idea Beats Lots of Small Ones'
before: Six Types of Investors — Which Group Are You In? (multi-idea)
after: The Secret of Making People Like You (single idea)
defect_named: 'overloaded with competing ideas', 'scattershot', 'thinly spread approach' (verbatim)
principle: One isolated core idea; 'Those that flopped were those that wandered.' (verbatim)
reason: Forde classified 90 of Schwab's 100 headlines as single-idea and found the same across 200+ swipe-file ads; no figures.

tested.result: 90/100 of Schwab's list single-idea; author's own promos: focused won, wandering flopped (no figures)

source: Marketing Examples, 'Bou's Near-Perfect Google ad' (Dave Trott's impact / communication / persuasion)
before: We're a brand agency
after: Ad that does all three parts: gets noticed, says what, says why (copy in image)
defect_named: Only 'communication' (what it is); no impact, no persuasion: reader's reaction 'No s***. I just googled that' (verbatim)
principle: Impact, then what, then why
reason: Bou's founder says it is their best performing ad (no metrics).

tested.result: vendor says best-performing ad; no figure

source: Marketing Examples, 'How Steve Jobs clarified Apple's message'
before: Lisa launch (1983): 'nine pages of geek speak' (Dry's description)
after: Think different.
quote_status: after verbatim; before is Dry's characterization
defect_named: 'geek speak'; 'Nobody outside NASA is interested' (verbatim)
principle: People buy the story, not the spec
reason: Lisa sold about 10,000 units (as stated); campaign ran five years. Not a controlled comparison.

tested.result: Lisa ~10,000 units; no figures for Think different

source: Copy Chief, 'The ONE sales hook that has never failed'
chief: Kevin Rogers (Copy Chief; author of post)
before: Hi, my school is new and needs furniture. Would you like to donate a couch and maybe some chairs? ... We'd really appreciate it.
after: No rewrite shown; fix: more 'you' statements than 'I' statements (check the you/I ratio), and segment by interest, desire or awareness
defect_named: Missing the one thing people care about: 'themselves' (verbatim); 'single dimensional, one size fits all messaging' (verbatim)
principle: WIIFM: the reader is the subject of every message
reason: Post claims opt-in 20% to 70% and other figures from segmentation; author's own claims, unverified and not tied to this email.

source: Copy Chief, 'How to Capture Drifting Attention with the Captain Hook Rule'
before: Hey, Captain Hook, I really need to tell –
after: Tick Tock Crocodile is coming! (or just 'Crocodile!')
defect_named: Hedging lead; the listener tunes out before the point
principle: 'Lead with the important stuff first.' (verbatim); explanation without an opening hook is 'hot air'
reason: Illustrative, not a tested pair.

source: NextAfter experiment #2759, National Breast Cancer Foundation
before: Email with no personalization (copy in image; two CTAs: donate and Facebook share)
after: Same email with first-name personalization
defect_named: Unaddressed reader
principle: Address the one reader by name
reason: NextAfter: the lift justified updating capture forms to collect first and last names (paraphrase).

tested.result: Click rate 0.19% to 0.72%, +270.1%, 100% confidence, n=29,389 (1,207 required), valid

source: NextAfter experiment, Bible League Canada Facebook ad CTA
before: Click to Learn More >>
after: Click to Give Bibles >>
defect_named: Indirect ask leaves the ad's purpose ambiguous
principle: A literal CTA that states the outcome of the click
reason: The direct ask 'aligned more strongly with donor intent and removed ambiguity about the ad's purpose' (verbatim); more clicks and higher conversion of clicks.

tested.result: Donor conversion 0.88% to 1.75%, +117.6%, 98.6% confidence, n=566,700 (172,555 required), valid

source: NextAfter experiment #189302, Time of Grace blog pages
before: Control blog page (copy in image)
after: 'Dear Reader' letter-style block added, offering a resource (T1 'How to fight anxiety', T2 'Mental Wellness'); copy in image
defect_named: Content page with no personal ask; cautionary: average gift fell from $135 to ~$30 as the offer shifted to email acquisition
principle: A personal, letter-style ask on content pages converts engaged readers; measure revenue, not only conversion
reason: 'users who are already engaged with Time of Grace content are more likely to provide their email' (verbatim).

source: MarketingExperiments (MECLABS), 'How do I write value-infused headlines?' (Ferguson Enterprises)
before: Exclusive Product And Event Information Delivered Right To Your Inbox!
after: Get The Ferguson Updates You Want, When You Want Them.
defect_named: Describes what the company sends, not what the subscriber gets
principle: State the value of the requested action from the customer's point of view
reason: Other page changes were made at the same time, so the headline alone cannot be credited (stated on page).

tested.result: +120% form submissions (page-level, multiple changes)

source: MarketingExperiments, 'value-infused headlines' (bank direct mail example)
before: National ad claim about having the most branches in the nation (wording not given)
after: We have a branch within walking distance of your home.
defect_named: A company-level claim where a prospect-level value was available
principle: Shift the headline to the value that matters to this prospect in this medium

source: Conversion Rate Experts, 'How to do guarantees right' (Geeks2U)
before: If you dislike our service… (negative 'get-out clause' framing; the client's actual first guarantee shown only as image)
after: We guarantee that you'll love our service.
defect_named: 'the most common guarantee mistake is negative wording' (paraphrase); a get-out clause instead of a promise
principle: A guarantee is a positive promise in one sentence with a simple visual
reason: Guarantee was among the most-viewed elements on the heat map (paraphrase). Sibling corpus holds the same test as a split-test record.

tested.result: Calls to sales +49% over the guarantee-less page; final version +24% conversions (as stated)
